content:
Facts: The surviving spouse, appointed heir limited to her reserved share under a holographic will, brought multiple claims against the deceased’s daughter and ex-wife, alleging that extensive lifetime transfers of money, securities, insurance premiums, and real estate constituted null or indirect donations, fictitious registrations, or undue payments, seeking reconstruction of the estate, collation, reduction for infringement of the reserved share, restitution of assets and fruits, and declaration of simulation of certain deeds.
Legal framework
Articles 536–564, 737–742, 751, 782–783, 2033 ICC on forced heirship, collation, reduction, nominalism, form of donations, modest value, undue payment; Articles 115, 183, 203 CPC on burden of proof, non-contestation and preclusions; principles on indirect donations, simulation, life insurance, prescription, division of inheritance, and valuation at division.
Interpretative issue
Whether transfers of securities and funds through joint or subsequently separated accounts qualify as indirect donations subject to collation; whether alleged donations are null for lack of form or exempt as gifts of modest value; whether a legatee is subject to collation; whether generic claims for reduction are admissible; whether withdrawals made during the deceased’s illness constitute undue payments; and how to reconstruct the estate considering relictum and donatum.
Principle applied
The division of a joint securities portfolio into separate accounts, consciously enriching a descendant, constitutes a valid indirect donation, subject to collation but not null for lack of form, and is governed by the nominalistic principle without revaluation. Facts generically contested or ambiguously admitted are deemed proven under Article 115 CPC. Donations of modest value are excluded from nullity for lack of public deed, assessed both objectively and in light of the donor’s standard of living. Collation applies automatically to spouses and descendants who are heirs, but not to mere legatees, including beneficiaries of life insurance policies. An action for reduction requires specific pleading of the estate, reserved share, and infringing acts and is inadmissible if proposed in a generic or hypothetical manner. Withdrawals from the deceased’s accounts lacking proof of justification constitute undue payments recoverable by the estate. Estate reconstruction must include relictum and collatable donations, with asset valuation fixed at the time of division. ID: ITI086; Instance_Type: First instance; Legal_Duration: P2Y9M; Law: IT – Civil Code – 542, 737, 751, 783, 1422; IT – Code of Civil Procedure – 91; State: IT; Type: Succession; Immovable_Assets: House, House, House, Garage; Movable_Assets: Money(941.146,44), Money (77.500,00), Financial assets, Bank account, Car, Furniture ; Type_of_succession: Testamentary; Second part of full text: €10,000.00 on 14/04/2006, from account (omissis) c/o Crédit Agricole. In addition to these transfers, totalling €242,000.00, the following can be added: credits to HEIR 2's current accounts of financial income deriving from securities registered to THE DECEASED for a total of €33,890.55 (page 17 of the Report); □ the transfer of securities totalling €9,000.00, which took place on 09/10/2019, from the BPER dossier; □ the transfer made on 22/09/2016 for €3,730.99 relating to the investment in gold, already commented on (see previous point 10 C.T.P. of the plaintiff)."; from the wording of the statement, the transfers which, according to the defendants, 'could' be considered donations must undoubtedly be considered donations, with all the consequences that this entails.
As specified by case law, in fact, "...the facts presented by the plaintiff as the basis for their claim...must be considered admitted, without the need for proof, if the party, in its statement of defence and response, has limited itself to an unclear and unspecific challenge" (Civil Court, Section 6 - 3, Order No. 26908 of 26/11/2020); the admission of a fact in a doubtful form cannot in fact be considered equivalent to a clear and specific challenge, which is required under Article 115 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure in order for a fact to be considered contested and therefore subject to proof. Therefore, donations received by the deceased from the defendant HEIR 2 must be considered admitted, for a total of €242,000.00 + €9,000.00 + €3,730.99 = €254,730.99; added to the previous figure of €525,119.90, the amount received by the defendant HEIR 2 as a gift from the deceased is €779,850.89.
With reference to the plaintiff's further allegations, the defendants' criticism of the plaintiff's indication of donations, which was 'by way of example but not exhaustive', appears to be worthy of consideration, for reasons entirely analogous to the above, regarding the need for clarity and specificity in the defence allegations. it is in fact up to the plaintiff, in compliance with the terms of preclusion, to provide a clear and exhaustive definition of the thema decidendum and probandum, as it is not otherwise possible to allow access to purely exploratory investigations. Therefore, only the arguments clearly formulated by the plaintiff should be taken into consideration, as specified below:

'the sums used by HEIR 2 in 2011 to pay off the mortgage contracted with ING Bank (approximately €73,500.00)'.

This circumstance is proven by the fact that, as documented (doc. 55 plaintiff), the sums came from the current account held in the name of the defendant but operated solely by THE DECEASED, no. (omissis), which, according to the plaintiff, was funded solely by resources attributable to THE DECEASED. The plaintiff adds that THE DECEASED himself declared himself to be the holder of account no. (omissis), and refers to doc. 90 for this purpose. This document contains a draft deed (the amount is not indicated) in which the account (omissis) is effectively indicated as 'held by THE DECEASED'; however, the document in question, which is incomplete, does not
Page14 of 28
appear decisive for the purposes of proving the plaintiff's claim, as this wording could also be due to a mere error;

'for the purchase of the property in Mariano Comense (approximately €110,000.00)'.

This sum is also attributed to the deceased as it comes from current account no. (omissis); the allegation cannot be accepted for the reasons given above;

"for the purchase of the property in Bellaria (€275,000.00)"

the plaintiff submits document 31 (purchase agreement) to the court, from which it can be inferred that the price was paid by bank drafts; the defendants submit documentation showing that these drafts were drawn on current account no. 30(omissis) in the name of HEIR 2 (a circumstance inferred by the defendants and not promptly contested by the plaintiff); the plaintiff's allegation on this point therefore appears to be without evidence and without foundation;

"as well as the direct credit to her Bper account of €100,000.00 (doc. no. 41)"

the credit is documented, and its nature as a gift must be inferred in the absence of clear allegations and evidence of a different title of attribution. The amount of €100,000.00 must therefore be calculated to arrive at an amount received by the defendant HEIR 2 as a gift from the deceased, amounting to €879,850.89;

all the divestments in the dossier (omissis) and the withdrawals from account no. (omissis), made also following the death of THE DECEASED and not going to the estate the account no. (omissis) in the name of HEIR 2 is not disputed; in the writ of summons, the plaintiff identifies a number of additional credits/disinvestments on this account which would demonstrate the fictitious nature of the account title (on which we have already expressed our opinion) or which would in any case constitute donations. Reference is made to the table on pages 15 and 16 of the writ of summons, which is reproduced here:

STIPULATION OF ARCAVITA POLICIES IN FAVOUR OF HEIR 2 €10,000.00 doc. 20
DEPOSIT TRANSFERS IN FAVOUR OF HEIR 2 €9,000.00 doc. 18
The above items are analysed below:

€29,395.55: on this point, the defendants, on page 50 of their statement of defence and response, argue as follows: 'On page 35, the plaintiff refers to other 'donations' as follows: €29,395.55 disinvestments from the securities deposit (omissis) in the name of THE DECEASED to the support current account (omissis) in the name of HEIR 2. The mere fact of the deposit has no probative value in terms of ownership of the financial asset, as can easily be deduced from the fact that the support account for the separate securities portfolios of HEIR 2 and THE DECEASED from 2001 to 2006 was account no. (omissis) in the name of the latter, while from 26/04/2006 to 09/02/2010 it was account (omissis) in the name of HEIR 2 alone."; the historical fact, i.e. the existence of the

Page16 of 28
divestment of securities pertaining to the securities deposit account in the name of THE DECEASED and settlement on the current account in the name of HEIR 2 alone is not disputed and is documented in doc. 36 of the plaintiff. The defendants, however, dispute that the plaintiff has adequately proven its claims. However, it should be noted that the Supreme Court has pointed out that "in civil proceedings, the generic inference of absence of evidence without denial of the historical fact is not equivalent to the specific dispute referred to in Article 115 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure." (Civil Cassation, Section 6 - 3, Order No. 17889 of 27/08/2020); significantly, the Cassation ruling referred to in the above maxim highlights that '...to say that there is no proof of a fact is not, in itself, equivalent to saying that that fact is to be considered disputed'; therefore, the mere dispute regarding the plaintiff's failure to meet the burden of proof does not appear to be effective, so that the amount in question must be counted as a donation; therefore, the amount received by the defendant HEIR 2 as a gift from the deceased is €909,246.44.

The item "TITLES FROM THE DOSSIER (omissis) AND INCLUDED IN THE DOSSIER
IN THE NAME OF HEIR 2" does not appear to warrant consideration, as it is already covered by the decision in paragraph 7).
Coupon credits for €32,800.00; the sum appears to be unsupported by documentary evidence (see plaintiff's doc. 46) and cannot be considered;
Transfer FROM THE DECEASED TO HEIR 2 ON 14.04.2006 TO THE ACCOUNT (omissis) for €10,000.00 documented in doc. 80; the amount has already been taken into consideration above, among the sums undisputedly admitted by the defendants;
TRANSFER FROM THE DECEASED TO HEIR 2 ON 29/02/2012 €15,000.00; according to the defendants, "the bank transfer made on 22/09/2012 for €15,000.00 is attributable to the repayment of a cash advance made by HEIR 2 to his father for the purchase of a car by the latter (Annex 6 - cheque made out to the car dealership THIRD PARTY 1 SRL in Cesena dated 03/05/2011)"; the payment is documented in doc. 15 of the plaintiff and is dated 29/02/2012. However, the different allocation attached by the defendants (loan repayment) is not documented, given that the cheque produced in doc. 8 does not prove the existence of a loan between the defendant and the deceased and is dated 3 May 2011, a date well before the bank transfer, and therefore the sum, which cannot be attributed otherwise, must be considered a gift and counted for inheritance purposes, resulting in an amount received by the defendant HEIR 2 as a gift from the deceased of €924,246.44.
TRANSFER FROM THE DECEASED TO HEIR 2 ON 5 November 2013 €5,000.00; this amount has already been taken into account above, among the sums undisputedly admitted by the defendants;

Page17 of 28

TRANSFER FROM THE DECEASED TO HEIR 2 ON 29.02.2016 € 3,730.99; the amount has already been taken into account above, among the sums undisputedly admitted by the defendants;
TRANSFER FROM THE DECEASED TO HEIR 2 ON 7 October 2019 €50,000.00; this amount has already been taken into account above, among the sums undisputedly admitted by the defendants;
TRANSFER FROM THE DECEASED TO HEIR 2 DATED 09.10.2019 €177,000.00: this amount has already been taken into account above, among the sums undisputedly admitted by the defendants;
CHEQUES ISSUED IN FAVOUR OF HEIR 2 €1,450.00 (doc. 66 plaintiff); the sum appears to be documented and not specifically contested by the counterparties, so that the amount received by the defendant HEIR 2 as a gift from the deceased is €925,646.44.
OTHER TRANSFERS FROM THE DECEASED TO HEIR 2 FROM 2012 TO 2020 €12,231.78: as can be seen from the narrative of the writ of summons, these are various transfers for the payment of nursery fees for HEIR 2's son, condominium fees, electricity and gas bills and various other expenses. In the defendants' opinion, these sums can reasonably be classified as modest contributions to maintenance attributable to the ordinary father-daughter-grandchild relationship and do not constitute gifts. The objection appears to be well-founded, given the purpose of these payments as stated in the plaintiff's narrative, taking into account the considerable length of time over which these payments were made and the modest amount of each payment.
WITHDRAWALS FROM THE DECEASED'S ACCOUNT MADE BY HEIR 2 WHILE THE FATHER WAS HOSPITALISED €6,000.00.

The defendants argue that these sums are attributable to expenses incurred by HEIR 2 for the care of his sick father; these withdrawals are therefore not disputed.
In the plaintiff's opinion, these withdrawals constitute liberal allocations, i.e. they are in any case without cause or justification and are therefore undue and must be returned to the estate; as can be seen from the documents produced by the plaintiff (docs. 17, 19, 78), the withdrawal was made by the defendant HEIR 2, limited to the amounts referred to in documents 17 and 19, while the withdrawal referred to in doc. 78 for €500.00 is attributable to HEIR 3. It is undisputed between the parties that these withdrawals took place when the father THE DECEASED was ill. On this point, as already assessed by the relevant case law (cf. Court of Appeal of Palermo, Section II, 03/05/2023, DeJure), reference to Article 1713 of the Italian Civil Code and the related obligation to render account appears relevant. On this point, the defendant merely alleged in general terms, without proving, that the sums were intended for the care of her sick father; therefore, in the absence of proof of the basis for the
Page18 of 28
withdrawal, with the consequent right of recovery from the estate, enforceable by the plaintiff in her capacity as heir, and therefore iure hereditario (cf. Article 2033 of the Italian Civil Code). It therefore seems possible to attribute to the defendant HEIR 2 (not as a donation subject to collation but as an undue payment to be returned to the estate), so that the amount received by the defendant HEIR 2 as a gift (or other) from the deceased amounts to €931,146.44.

TRANSFERS MADE BY HEIR 2 USING HOME BANKING ON THE ACCOUNT
OF THE FATHER €1,903.20; this sum cannot be taken into account, given that it appears undisputed between the parties that it was used to pay the fees owed to the deceased's solicitor, THIRD PARTY 2 (doc. 81, defendant's file).
STIPULATION OF ARCAVITA POLICIES IN FAVOUR OF HEIR 2 €10,000.00: the amount appears to be
peacefully taken into consideration by the defendant itself (page 62 of the statement of defence) and must therefore be counted as a donation in favour of HEIR 2, to obtain the amount in his favour of €941,146.44.
GIRO DEPOSITS IN FAVOUR OF HEIR 2 €9,000.00: the amount is admitted by the defendant and has already been calculated as above. The transfer of €10,000.00 on 14 April 2006 is also undisputedly admitted and has already been calculated.
Finally, on the basis of what can be reconstructed from the plaintiff's substantial narrative, it remains to analyse the transfer of €5,000.00 made to HEIR 2 on 5 November 2013, which, according to the plaintiff, constitutes a loan made by the deceased and never repaid by the debtor. The amount has already been calculated as above, as it has been admitted by the defendant as a donation.


"order HEIR 3 to return the sums credited to her and originating from account no. (omissis) as null and void donations (exceeding the modest value), quantified as no less than €20,000.00, subject to better quantification at the outcome of the preliminary investigation."

The first argument put forward by the plaintiff concerns the alleged nullity of the donations received by the defendant HEIR 3 due to a defect in form. The argument appears unfounded, as can be inferred from the plaintiff's own narrative (see pages 22 and 23 of the writ of summons), which quantifies the amount allegedly donated to the defendant HEIR 3 of €52,222.69, which, however, was obtained by adding up numerous payments which, taken individually, certainly do not exceed the limit of modest value (Article 783 of the Italian Civil Code), both from an objective point of view and taking into account, from a subjective point of view, the high standard of living that the plaintiff herself attributes to the deceased during his lifetime; the claim must therefore be rejected.
Page19 of 28

"Include the above gratuitous attributions in the total value of the estate, attributing them, by virtue of collation, to the share due to HEIR 2, reducing them starting from the most recent ones until the legitimate share due to HEIR 1 is reinstated."

In this regard, the plaintiff appears to express her intention to take action by requesting a reduction in donations due to infringement of legitimate rights. The difference between a request for collation and an action for reduction due to infringement of legitimate rights appears clear and well established in legislation and case law. On this point, recent case law has clarified that 'While reduction sacrifices the donees to the extent necessary to restore the legitimate portion that has been infringed and is therefore based on the relationship between the legitimate portion and the disposable portion, collation, in the relationships indicated in Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code, places the donated asset, in proportion to the inheritance share of each, in common among the co- heirs who are the spouse or descendants of the deceased, including the donee, without any regard to the distinction between legitimate and disposable assets. Nevertheless, the fact that collation may in fact eliminate any infringement of the legitimate portion, allowing the legitimate heirs to obtain equal proportions in the division, does not exclude the possibility that the legitimate heir may simultaneously bring an action for reduction against the co-heir donee, given that only the acceptance of such a claim ensures that the aggrieved legitimate heir is reinstated to his or her reserved share with the allocation of assets in kind, depriving the co-heirs of the right to opt for the imputation of the relative value. At the same time, and conversely, it must be recognised that the action for reduction, once exercised, does not exclude the effectiveness of collation with regard to the donation subject to reduction, it being understood that while collation, when requested exclusively, entails the return of the donated asset to the estate, without regard to the distinction between legitimate and disposable, in the case of concurrence with the action for reduction, it intervenes at a later stage, after the legitimate portion has been reinstated, in order to redistribute any surplus, i.e. the additional value of the gift that expresses the disposable portion'. (Civil Cassation Section 2 - Judgment No. 28196 of 10/12/2020 (Rv. 659836 - 01). For the purposes of exercising the action for reduction, however, the legitimate heir '...must indicate the extent to which his or her reserved share has been infringed, determining the exact value of the estate and the value of the infringed legitimate share, and must, to this end, attach and prove, even by resorting to simple presumptions, provided that they are serious, precise and consistent, all the elements necessary to establish whether, and to what extent, the reserved share has been infringed" (Court of Bari, Section I, 03/01/2022, No. 35, DeJure); in the present case, however, the action for reduction appears to be only generically proposed by the plaintiff, in a vague and hypothetical manner, lacking specific proposals (regarding the identification of the infringing provision, the extent of the estate, the extent of the infringement, etc.). The claim cannot therefore be upheld. As specified in the above-mentioned case law, in any case, this does not prejudice the exercise of division and collation, even if this were to result, in practical terms, in the reinstatement of any injury.
Page20 of 28

"in any case, ascertain and declare that the substantial bank transfers made by THE DECEASED during his lifetime, as specified in the narrative, to HEIR 2 and HEIR 3, are to be considered null and void due to lack of formal requirements, as they are bank transfers, cheques and giro deposits made without a public deed";

the request for a declaration of nullity of the donations to HEIR 3 has already been discussed in sub-paragraph 9); similarly, the transfer of securities referred to in the aforementioned files has already been discussed in sub-paragraph 5). With regard to the remaining donations to HEIR 2, already discussed in paragraph 8), nullity due to lack of form can be ruled out, as these are, at most, donations of modest value (taking into account the undisputed high standard of living of the deceased); as regards the transfer of securities, the amount of €525,119.90 has already been discussed in sub-paragraph 7), qualifying it as an indirect donation.
However, attention must be paid to the transfer of €177,000.00 made on 9 October 2019 from the account (omissis) at Crédit Agricole, which is the only one that does not appear at first glance to be attributable to a donation of modest value (doc. 14 plaintiff). There is no dispute (indeed, there is unanimous admission) on the part of the defendants that this is a donation. Moreover, as mentioned above, this donation had already been attributed to the estate by virtue of collation. This donation must also be declared null and void. It should also be noted that 'The possible nullity of the donation made by the deceased, if declared by the court, does not, for the purposes of division, produce results that are dissimilar to collation, but only more radical, in that it returns to the estate of the deceased, as if they had never left it, given that, under the law, the effects of a null and void contract, and therefore also the property transfers made under it, are considered never to have taken place' (Civil Court, Section 2 - Order No. 15666 of 11/06/2019). The effects of nullity, therefore, are not dissimilar to those already specified above. Since this is a case of nullity, the relevant claim is not subject to a limitation period (Article 1422 of the Italian Civil Code).

"include in the inheritance the premiums paid by THE DECEASED in relation to the life insurance policies taken out for the benefit of HEIR 2 (for a total of €10,000.00) and HEIR 3 (for a total of €30,709.86)";

The life insurance policies in favour of HEIR 2 have already been discussed.
As regards the premiums paid for the life insurance policies in favour of HEIR 3, in the plaintiff's opinion, they constitute a donation subject to the obligation of collation. The defendants object that Ms HEIR 3, not being an heir, would not be required to collate (see page 52 of the statement of defence and reply). From an analysis of the will (plaintiff's document 1), it is clear that Ms. HEIR 3 is a legatee, while Ms. HEIR 2 and Ms. HEIR 1 are heirs, according to the shares established by the deceased. Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code establishes that children and their descendants, as well as the spouse, who are involved in the succession are required to make a collation. Therefore, the universal successor who falls within the subjects indicated by specific legal provision (Court)
Page21 of 28
Pavia, 20/01/1989, DeJure). In the case in question, Ms HEIR 3 is not one of the persons referred to in Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code, nor is she a universal successor, being merely a legatee. Therefore, the request for the collation of the premiums and additional donations made by the deceased to Ms HEIR 3 cannot be accepted.

"also include in the estate the property located in Cesena (FC), via (omissis), as transferred by the deceased to HEIR 2 (for bare ownership) by way of anticipated succession, and to HEIR 3 (for life usufruct) free of charge; the property located in Cesena (FC), via (omissis), as the marital home purchased by HEIR 1 and THE DECEASED with the latter's money; the property located in Cesena (FC), via (omissis), together with the garage, located in Via (omissis), as the subject of succession mortis causa and indicated in the will, as well as the garage located in Cesena (FC), via Martiri d'Ungheria, estimating the value of said properties at the time of the opening of the succession";


with regard to the property in Cesena, Via (omissis), the relevant notarial deed (doc. 3 plaintiff's file), containing a stipulation in favour of a third party to which Ms HEIR 2, in that capacity, adhered, establishes in Article 8 that '...the transfer in favour of the daughter takes place by way of anticipated succession'; the wording appears clear and, moreover, cannot be traced back to divorce settlement agreements, as it concerns the daughter and not the relationship between the spouses. The property, therefore, limited to bare ownership, must be included in the estate; this does not apply to the usufruct, as the defendant HEIR 3 is not subject to collation;
there are no disputes regarding the inclusion of the property in Via (omissis) in the estate, as it was purchased with the deceased's money; to be precise, also on the basis of the wording of the will, 'the flat, the garage and the furniture therein' must be transferred to the estate: in fact, as specified by case law, 'In the event of the purchase of a property with the testator's own money and registration in the name of another person, whom the testator intends to benefit in this way, the sale constitutes a formal instrument for the transfer of the asset and the corresponding enrichment of the recipient's assets and, therefore, constitutes - also for the purposes of collation - an indirect donation of the asset itself and not of the money' (Civil Court, Section 2, Judgment No. 13619 of 30/05/2017);
are finally included in the inheritance, as per the declaration of succession (doc. 18 defendant's file): the property located in Cesena (FC), via (omissis), together with the garage, located in Via (omissis), the garage located in Cesena (FC), via Martiri d'Ungheria;


"order the defendants to return the proceeds received from the title to the inherited real estate attributed to them by the deceased"

Page22 of 28
the plaintiff alleges on page 40 of the introductory act that 'Immediately after the publication of the will, the defendants took ownership of the apartment in the manner described above, in order to receive the benefits thereof (doc. no. 71): the property in Via Versilia (with a total value of €135,000.00) had, in fact, already been leased in 2009 by the deceased, with periodic renewals of the lease agreement, with a monthly rent of €420.00 (doc. no. 61); not only must the property be included in the estate as part of the relictum, but also the fruits received by HEIR 2 and HEIR 3 since the legal claim was filed, pursuant to Article 561 of the Italian Civil Code, must be returned in the event of a reduction in the relevant testamentary disposition as it is detrimental to the legitimate share"; the claim, made pursuant to Article 561 of the Italian Civil Code, appears unfounded and must be rejected, as a result of the rejection of the related claim for reduction.

Ascertain and declare that the deed of transfer drawn up by Notary THIRD PARTY 3 no. rep. (omissis) conceals a donation, as it is in fact a deed for no consideration.

The question appears unfounded. In fact, a reading of the document itself shows that there is no difference between the expressed intention and the desired effect; as specified by case law, relative simulation implies "...the divergence between the declared statement and the intended statement and, therefore, the existence of two legal transactions': the simulated transaction and the concealed transaction (Civil Court, Section 3, Judgment No. 1523 of 26/01/2010); in the present case (doc. 3 plaintiff's file), the attribution to HEIR 2 exactly complies with the intention expressed in the deed to assign the asset by way of anticipated succession. As regards HEIR 3, the attribution is part of the context of reciprocal services, established in the deed, consistent with the intention expressed therein to settle the financial relations between the spouses in view of the imminent divorce.

Reconstruction of the estate - dissolution of the community property Prior to the dissolution of the community property, the estate must be reconstructed on the basis of the above considerations and the documentation in the deeds (docs. 17, 18, inventory report and inheritance declaration, defendant's file), which must take into account the relictum and donations specified above; in fact, as highlighted in the relevant case law, 'In the presence of donations made during the lifetime of the deceased, the collation of the estate is a legal instrument aimed at forming the estate to be divided in order to ensure balance and equal treatment between the various co-heirs, so as not to alter the value ratio between the various shares, to be determined in relation to the extent of each co-heir's right, on the basis of the sum of the 'relictum' and the 'donatum' at the time of the opening of the succession, and thus guarantee each of the heirs the possibility of obtaining a quantity of assets proportionate to their share. It follows that the obligation of collation arises automatically upon the opening of the succession and that the donated assets must be contributed regardless of an express request by the co-heirs, as

Page23 of 28
sufficient for this purpose is the request for division and the mention therein of the existence of certain assets, forming part of the estate to be reconstructed, as the subject of a previous donation' (Court of Palermo, Section II, 18/06/2019, DeJure).
The estate shall therefore be determined as follows: ESTATE ASSETS: - property in Cesena, via (omissis), limited to bare ownership;

property located in Cesena (FC), Via (omissis) (apartment, garage and furnishings, as identified in the inventory report);
property located in Cesena (FC), Via (omissis), together with the garage located in Via (omissis); - garage located in Cesena (FC), Via Martiri d'Ungheria;
€941,146.44, to be allocated to the estate by HEIR 2 for the above securities;
Bper Banca securities deposit no. (omissis)
current account balance at Bper Banca no. (omissis);
Volkswagen Polo with registration number (omissis);
Movable property in general as indicated in the inventory report;

In the opinion of the defendants, the substantial donations received by the plaintiff, as detailed in the conclusions, should also be taken into account: '- €112,257.00 (table on page 8 CTP) - €220,869.00 (table on page 8 CTP) - €22,500.00 (table on page 9 CTP) - €93,356.00 (table on page 9 CTP) - as per the summary table on page 37 CTP for a total of €448,426.00"; in particular (see pages 7 et seq. of the defendants' technical report, Annex A); however, with regard to the amount of €112,257.00, the defendants also tend to combine various sums, which are modest in amount when taken individually (doc. 1 defendant's file) and which therefore may well fall within the normal dynamics of married life (the plaintiff and the deceased were married since 2003), such as maintenance expenses, donations of modest value or contributions to the family household, which are certainly not subject to collation. The sum of €220,869.00 refers to the purchase of the property in Via Tommaseo, already considered above. The sum of €22,500.00 (Annex 3), relating to the subscription to a pension fund in favour of the plaintiff by the deceased, it can be considered a form of enrichment, likely dictated by a spirit of generosity, as it is unrelated to family expenses and dynamics and cannot be considered a donation of modest value, but rather aimed at enriching, at the expense of the settlor, the assets of the beneficiary. Furthermore, with reference to the amount
Page24 of 28

"Include the above gratuitous attributions in the total value of the estate, attributing them, by virtue of collation, to the share due to HEIR 2, reducing them starting from the most recent ones until the legitimate share due to HEIR 1 is reinstated."

In this regard, the plaintiff appears to express her intention to take action by requesting a reduction in donations due to infringement of legitimate rights. The difference between a request for collation and an action for reduction due to infringement of legitimate rights appears clear and well established in legislation and case law. On this point, recent case law has clarified that 'While reduction sacrifices the donees to the extent necessary to restore the legitimate portion that has been infringed and is therefore based on the relationship between the legitimate portion and the disposable portion, collation, in the relationships indicated in Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code, places the donated asset, in proportion to the inheritance share of each, in common among the co- heirs who are the spouse or descendants of the deceased, including the donee, without any regard to the distinction between legitimate and disposable assets. Nevertheless, the fact that collation may in fact eliminate any infringement of the legitimate portion, allowing the legitimate heirs to obtain equal proportions in the division, does not exclude the possibility that the legitimate heir may simultaneously bring an action for reduction against the co-heir donee, given that only the acceptance of such a claim ensures that the aggrieved legitimate heir is reinstated to his or her reserved share with the allocation of assets in kind, depriving the co-heirs of the right to opt for the imputation of the relative value. At the same time, and conversely, it must be recognised that the action for reduction, once exercised, does not exclude the effectiveness of collation with regard to the donation subject to reduction, it being understood that while collation, when requested exclusively, entails the return of the donated asset to the estate, without regard to the distinction between legitimate and disposable, in the case of concurrence with the action for reduction, it intervenes at a later stage, after the legitimate portion has been reinstated, in order to redistribute any surplus, i.e. the additional value of the gift that expresses the disposable portion'. (Civil Cassation Section 2 - Judgment No. 28196 of 10/12/2020 (Rv. 659836 - 01). For the purposes of exercising the action for reduction, however, the legitimate heir '...must indicate the extent to which his or her reserved share has been infringed, determining the exact value of the estate and the value of the infringed legitimate share, and must, to this end, attach and prove, even by resorting to simple presumptions, provided that they are serious, precise and consistent, all the elements necessary to establish whether, and to what extent, the reserved share has been infringed" (Court of Bari, Section I, 03/01/2022, No. 35, DeJure); in the present case, however, the action for reduction appears to be only generically proposed by the plaintiff, in a vague and hypothetical manner, lacking specific proposals (regarding the identification of the infringing provision, the extent of the estate, the extent of the infringement, etc.). The claim cannot therefore be upheld. As specified in the above-mentioned case law, in any case, this does not prejudice the exercise of division and collation, even if this were to result, in practical terms, in the reinstatement of any injury.

Therefore, the plaintiff must allocate the total amount of €77,500.00 to the estate for collation. The case must then proceed, as per the following order, for the purposes of valuation and actual division, taking into account that said valuation must be made with reference to the value at the date of division; in fact, '...in the judgment of dissolution of the joint ownership of the estate, the valuation for the formation of the shares of the jointly owned assets must be made at the time of division...' (Civil Court, Section 6 - 2, Order no. 5993 of 04/03/2020).
